html:
A bold experiment in France from 1716 to 1720, when the Scottish financier John Law tried to fix the crown's huge debts with paper money and a giant trading company. It ended in one of the first great financial crashes.

Louis XIV had left France deep in debt. The regent, the Duke of Orléans, let Law open a bank in 1716 that issued paper notes. Law then took over the Mississippi Company, which held the trade of French Louisiana, merged it with other trading companies and had it take on the state's debt. People paid for shares with government bonds and paper money. The share price soared in 1719.

The bank printed ever more notes to keep the price up. In 1720 people began to swap notes and shares for gold and silver, and the system collapsed. Law fled the country.

The Mississippi Bubble burst the same year as the South Sea Bubble in London. It showed money could be created, and it left the French wary of banks and bank notes for decades.
sum: A bold experiment in France from 1716 to 1720, when the Scottish financier John Law tried to fix the crown's huge debts with paper money and a giant trading company. It ended in one of the first great financial crashes.
